name: Aaron Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've been at Routewise for five years, which is a software company that makes stock systems for warehouses. I look after the old inventory module, the bit that tracks pallets in and out. Most days I'm fixing reports that don't add up, like a warehouse in the north showing minus forty pallets of tinned tomatoes. I like that I know the system better than almost anyone. What wears me out is when sales promise customers features that don't exist yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. I tried one once because my team lead asked, and it gave me code that looked fine and was wrong in a way that took me a day to find. Since then I just don't bother. I live with my partner Leah, she's a dental hygienist, and we've got about four months saved plus a car loan we're paying off. I play five-a-side football on Tuesdays and that's about as exciting as my week gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me, to be honest. I've never been convinced. I'd be fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much. Maybe at lunch I'd say, see, the old system still needs someone who knows it. I'm not one for posting online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased. Nobody wants to touch the old inventory module except me, and that keeps my job safe. Routewise has steady customers and we're not a flashy company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Keep paying off the car, keep the savings where they are. Maybe ask for a small raise at my review in April, since I'd be the guy who knows the old code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty much how I feel now. Just normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still nag at you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, a bit. Eighteen months left. And Leah wants to buy a flat eventually, which feels a long way off on our money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the team lead who asked you to try the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably keep nudging. She's not pushy, she just likes new things. I'd tell her the inventory module isn't the place to experiment, and she'd let it go.

say: I'd say the **old system** still needs someone who actually knows it.
I'd keep it to **lunch chat** rather than posting online.
think: I privately feel **safe**, since nobody else wants the inventory module.
Routewise has **steady customers** and isn't a flashy company.
do: Carry on with the **inventory module** exactly as now.
Keep paying off the **car loan**, with eighteen months left.
Ask for a **small raise** at the April review.
feel: He feels **calm**, much like normal life.
S0.quote: Nobody wants to touch the old inventory module except me, and that keeps my job safe.
fieldNote: His sense of safety rests on being the **only one** who knows an old system.
A single bad experience turned him **off AI tools** for good.
His worries are **ordinary ones**: a car loan and a far-off flat.

steps.text: Keep maintaining Routewise's inventory module without AI tools
Keep paying the car loan and hold savings steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Coding's on the list. And checking. That's most of what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something sensible, like we'll have to see how it goes. I'd say the tools still make mistakes, and someone has to catch them. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it would worry me. If AI can read the old code faster than I can, then being the only guy who knows the inventory module stops being worth much. I'm average at my job, I know that, and average is what gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe an extra two hundred a month, and pay the car off early if I could. I'd wait a bit to see what Routewise actually does before I changed anything. I probably wouldn't touch the AI tools until I was told to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Quietly. I'd probably go quiet at home, and Leah would notice before I said anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leah say when she noticed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask what's wrong and I'd say nothing, and then two days later I'd tell her. She'd say her job is fine, nobody's replacing a hygienist with a chatbot. She'd be right, which helps and also doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to be told to use the tools. What if being told comes too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the risk. I know waiting isn't a great plan. I just don't like jumping first, and I've seen people jump into things that went nowhere.

say: I'd say we'll **have to see**, since the tools still make **mistakes**.
I wouldn't make a fuss in public or online.
think: I privately fear my **only-one-who-knows** advantage stops counting.
I'm **average** at my job, and average is what gets replaced.
do: Save an extra **two hundred a month** and pay the car off early.
Wait to see what **Routewise** actually does before changing anything.
Hold off on **AI tools** until a manager tells him to use them.
feel: He feels quietly **anxious** and goes **quiet at home**.
S1.quote: I'm average at my job, I know that, and average is what gets replaced.
fieldNote: He's honest that **waiting** is a weak plan but sticks with it.
His partner's **hygienist job** gives the household a safety net.
His worry shows at home before he **says it out loud**.

steps.text: Save an extra 200 a month and pay off the car loan early
Wait to see Routewise's plans before learning AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's out of our hands and the government will have to sort out what happens to people. I'd probably say it calmly. I'm not a placard person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd expect to be gone by 2028, maybe earlier. Everything I do is at a screen, so the robots coming later means nothing for me. The only lucky bit is Leah's job is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away: no new car, no holiday, cheaper phone. I'd put everything into savings. And I'd talk with Leah about living on her pay for a while, which isn't something I ever pictured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel useless, if I'm honest. Five years of knowing that module, and it counts for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would living on Leah's pay look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Her pay covers rent and bills, and not much more. We'd shelve buying a flat. My parents might help a bit, but they're not well off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at a different job at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something in a warehouse, actually, since I know how they run from the software side. That's hands-on for a few more years. Going from writing the warehouse stock system to scanning the pallets myself would be strange.

say: I'd say it's **out of our hands** and the government must sort it out.
I'd say it calmly; I'm **not a placard person**.
think: I privately expect to be **gone by 2028**, maybe sooner.
All my work is at a **screen**, so the robot delay means nothing for me.
do: Cut back hard with **no holiday** and a cheaper phone plan.
Plan with Leah to live on her **hygienist pay** for a while.
Look at **warehouse jobs**, using what he knows from the software side.
feel: He feels **alarmed** and **useless**, as five years of knowledge stops counting.
S2.quote: Going from writing the warehouse stock system to scanning the pallets myself would be strange.
fieldNote: He shifts responsibility to **government**, not out of ideology but resignation.
His partner's **hands-on job** becomes the household's lifeline.
His fallback of **warehouse work** is grounded in what he already knows.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and switch to a cheaper phone plan
Live on Leah's hygienist pay with some help from his parents
Apply for warehouse jobs that use his stock-system knowledge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a bit more room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to plan, so companies should be telling staff what they intend. I'd ask our managers straight out at the next all-hands what the plan is for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd lose the job around 2030 or 2031. But five years means I could get the car paid off and the savings up first. I'd probably have to start using the tools, even though I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally start using the AI tools at work, slowly, on small reports, so I'm not the last one. I'd push savings up to six months and finish the car loan. I'd also ask about moving into the implementation team, the people who go out and set up Routewise in actual warehouses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more manageable. I'd have time to get my house in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the implementation team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're on site, talking to warehouse managers and fixing things in person. It's half people, half software. I reckon that lasts longer than sitting with the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to actually start using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody showing me it works on our code, not on some demo. If my mate Callum got the AI tool working on our inventory reports, I'd give it a go, because Callum is careful like me.

say: I'd say companies should **tell staff** their plans while there's time.
I'd ask managers straight out at the **all-hands** meeting.
think: I privately expect to lose the job around **2030 or 2031**.
Five years lets me **clear the car** and build savings first.
do: Start using **AI tools** slowly on small inventory reports.
Push savings to **six months** and finish the car loan.
Ask to move into the **implementation team** that sets up warehouses on site.
feel: He feels **anxious** but more in control, with time to get his house in order.
S3.quote: If my mate Callum got the AI tool working on our inventory reports, I'd give it a go, because Callum is careful like me.
fieldNote: Five years is enough to move him to **reluctant learning**.
He trusts a **careful colleague** more than any demo.
He sees **on-site implementation** as the part of software that lasts.

steps.text: Try AI tools on small inventory reports once Callum shows they work
Finish the car loan and build savings to six months
Ask to join the implementation team that sets up warehouses on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people shouldn't panic. I'd say it's like any big change: the sensible thing is to plan steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes it easy to do nothing, and I know that's my habit. I'd probably carry on for four or five years before I moved. The job still goes in the end, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Routewise for now and keep saving. I'd probably buy a flat with Leah in the next few years, while I still have a solid job, because getting a mortgage later would be harder. Then around 2030 I'd look at what's left and decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but faint. It's there, just not loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a flat is a big commitment if your income might go. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But Leah's job is the steadier one, and we'd buy something small. If my partner Leah and I wait to buy a flat, we might never get a mortgage at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2036, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe managing a warehouse team, or still at Routewise doing whatever's left. I'm not good at picturing that far ahead.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time**, so people shouldn't panic.
I'd call for **steady planning**, like any big change.
think: I privately know ten years makes it easy for me to **do nothing**.
The job still **goes in the end**, even with more time.
do: Carry on at **Routewise** for four or five more years.
Buy a **small flat** with Leah while both incomes are solid.
Wait until around **2030** to decide on a new direction.
feel: He feels a faint, quiet **anxiety** that isn't loud.
S4.quote: If my partner Leah and I wait to buy a flat, we might never get a mortgage at all.
fieldNote: The long warning pulls forward a **house purchase**, not a career change.
He admits his **habit of delay** openly.
He **can't picture** 2036, which is honest for someone his age.

steps.text: Buy a small flat with Leah while both have steady jobs
Wait until around 2030 before choosing a new career direction
Keep working on Routewise's inventory module for now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to do anything except cut back and lean on Leah. What would help is clear notice from employers, like a year's warning, and some decent unemployment pay while you work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be average. Everyone talks about the brilliant people or the people at the bottom. People like me in the middle just get on with it, and we'd get hit too.

headlineQuote: People like me in the middle just get on with it, and we'd get hit too.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** developer who has maintained one warehouse **inventory module** for five years.
He lives with **Leah**, a dental hygienist, has four months saved and a car loan.
He **never uses AI** after one bad experience, and prefers to wait and see.
He's calm in AI Plateau but **alarmed** by fast AGI, relying on Leah's hands-on job.
With more time he'd **reluctantly** learn the tools and move toward on-site work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's **no time** to do anything but cut back and lean on Leah.
whatWouldHelp: A **year's notice** from employers before cuts.
Decent **unemployment pay** while he works out what's next.
